cells.title: The draft sets a target for free cash itself

why.text: Today: no target for free cash. Draft: certifications of five to seven percent of the budget each year, reached through conservative revenue estimates and budget turnbacks.

measures.label: Today, on the latest free cash

cells.title: The draft splits every year’s free cash by rule

why.text: Today: top up general stabilization to five percent, then at least 10% to the OPEB trust, then the special purpose fund, then any one-time use. Draft: a minimum share for each of six uses.

cells.title: A wider band and a yearly deposit

why.text: Today: at least five percent of the budget, all stabilization funds together no more than ten percent. Draft: five to eight percent, plus a set deposit every year.

measures.label: Draft
measures.value: At most a third; refill in 2

measures.label: In practice, Town Meeting votes held

cells.title: Harder to draw, sooner to refill

why.text: Both: emergencies, ideally only above five percent, by a two-thirds vote. Draft adds: below it, take no more than one third, and refill within two years, not three.

cells.title: A target for the special funds together

why.text: Today: a deposit sized in each year’s capital planning. Draft: three to five percent of the budget across the funds, and at least 10% of free cash.

cells.title: Town Meeting sets each fund’s purpose

why.text: Today’s rule asks two thirds to spend from any stabilization fund. State law asks a majority for a special purpose fund. The draft sets no vote.
Today: $50,000, and no more than one half of one percent of the budget. The draft does not size the Finance Committee’s reserve fund at all.

measures.label: State law
measures.value: Up to 5% of last year’s levy

cells.title: Transfers stay with the Finance Committee

why.text: State law: up to five percent of last year’s levy, for extraordinary or unforeseen costs, transferred by the Finance Committee. The draft adds nothing.

cells.title: Ten percent becomes a step toward full funding

why.text: Today: at least 10% of certified free cash each year. Draft: keeps the 10% as one option, and states an intention to pay the full actuarially determined contribution.

cells.title: Current retirees stay on the budget

why.text: Today: the trust does not pay current retirees, and moving money in or out takes a Town Meeting vote. The draft adds a valuation every two years.

cells.title: A yearly amount for capital in cash

why.text: Today: a project is anything over $20,000; no spending level. Draft: two to three percent of the budget, net of debt, in cash each year, and 20% to 30% of free cash.

cells.title: Borrow only for large, long-lived projects

why.text: Both: long-term debt only for projects over $100,000 with at least ten years of life.

cells.title: Maturing debt keeps its place in the budget

why.text: Draft: when a non-excluded bond is paid off and not replaced, its yearly payment goes to a special purpose fund. Today’s rule has no such step.

measures.label: In practice
measures.value: 5.83% of the budget, all debt, FY2025

cells.title: A different base for the limits

why.text: Today: limits as a share of the tax levy (4% regular, 14% all). Draft: of the general fund budget (2% to 4% within the levy, 5% to 11% all, of operating revenues).

cells.title: Receipts capped at last year’s collections

why.text: Today: no written rule. Draft: local receipts estimated at no more than 90% of last year’s collections without firm evidence, and each forecast checked against the year that followed.
The draft says estimates set too low leave excess revenue that cannot help the public in the year it comes in.

note.text: Money in is what is set aside before a budget is drawn up. Money out is what a fund may pay for, and the vote it takes. The verdicts are our reading of the two documents.

links.label: Who has argued for each direction, meeting by meeting

paragraphs.text: This project recommends neither direction: not to save more, and not to spend more. It shows what each setting would do to figures the town has already published. The boards decide.
The draft itself says its targets are recommended for towns like Lunenburg, and that the town is to test them against its own finances before adopting them.
